title: Unkechaug Indian Reservation
summary: The Unkechaug Indian Nation is a Native nation recognized by New York State and centered on the Poospatuck Reservation along Poospatuck Creek in Mastic. The reservation is a continuing homeland where Unkechaug people maintain government, community, language work, and relationships with land and water.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Unkechaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: Poospatuck is a living Unkechaug homeland and seat of government, not a remnant of a disappeared people. Its history connects land defense, state law, family continuity, language revitalization, and present-day Native sovereignty on Long Island.
introduction_content: The Unkechaug Indian Nation has maintained a community at Poospatuck on the Mastic Peninsula through centuries of land pressure and outside attempts to deny Native identity. New York law recognizes the Poospatuck (Unkechauge) Indian Nation, while federal agencies do not currently list the Nation as federally recognized.1
history_content:
When English settlement expanded into Brookhaven in the 1650s, Unkechaug homelands extended across several thousand acres in the southern part of the town. The reservation's continuing land base comes from a July 2, 1700 agreement in which William Tangier Smith set aside 175 acres in four parcels for Unkechaug families and their descendants. Fifty acres along Poospatuck Creek remained the community's home base.1

Later encroachment and disputed transfers reduced the land held by Unkechaug families. Community members defended the reservation through their own government, New York courts, and relationships among families. In Matter of Spota v. Jackson (2008), the New York Court of Appeals again described the Unkechaug Nation as recognized by New York State and the Poospatuck land as an Indian reservation.2

Unkechaug people have also preserved community history in print, schools, oral knowledge, legal advocacy, and language work. In 2017, Chief Harry Wallace joined Stephanie Fielding and Tina Tarrant in a Stony Brook University language program connecting surviving Long Island vocabularies with related Eastern Algonquian languages.

References

  • John A. Strong, The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island: A History (2011).
  • New York Indian Law, Article 10: Poospatuck (Unkechauge) Indian Nation.
  • Matter of Spota v. Jackson, 10 N.Y.3d 46 (2008).
translation_content:
Unkechaug has been interpreted as “people from beyond the hill.” Poospatuck is the place name associated with the reservation and creek; historical writing sometimes used the two names interchangeably, although one names the Nation and the other names its homeland.

Thomas Jefferson recorded 202 words from Unkechaug speakers during his 1791 visit. Smaller word lists were recorded later from community members, including Mesh Bradley and Martha Maynes. These vocabularies preserve only fragments of a living language tradition interrupted by colonial pressure.1

Language revitalization continues through Unkechaug leadership and collaboration with speakers and teachers of related Eastern Algonquian languages.
land_loss_content: In exchange for reconfirming previous land deeds between the Unkechaug and colonist Colonel William Tangier Smith, Smith granted in perpetuity one hundred and seventy-five acres of land to the tribe on Mastic Neck. The grant stated that the Unkechaug, "their children and the posterity of their children forever shall without molestation from me or my heirs or assigns shall and may plant and sowe forever" and added that the Indians could not sell, convey, or alienate this planting right or any part thereof to any persons whatsoever. The bounds of the deed were unfortunately blurred, and the Unkechaug now only retain fifty of the original one hundred and seventy-five acres, including the tract of the historic William Floyd Estate. Unkechaug people are recorded as living on the estate during the early 1700s and later archaeological reports confirm wigwam and planting grounds.
